title: Language policy of the Czech Republic in the field of second foreign language teaching – the future of German, Spanish, French, Russian, and Italian in the revision of curriculum proposal
text:
Language policy of the Czech Republic in the field of second foreign language teaching – the future of German, Spanish, French, Russian, and Italian in the revision of curriculum proposal

Olga Nadvornikova

1

– Tomas Klinka

DOI: 10.18355/XL.2023.16.04.12

Abstract 
The study describes the context of foreign language teaching in the Czech Republic 
over the last ten years. Special interest is given to the area of teaching second foreign 
languages (FL2). The aim is to show to what extent the intentions of the Czech state 
in this area serve as a possible vector for implementing the ideas of the European 
Union and the Council of Europe in language policy and, on the contrary, how they 
may pose a threat to those ideas. The text includes statistical data, analyses of risks 
and opportunities, and expert suggestions for future language policy solutions. 
Key words: second foreign language, language policy, curriculum, Czech education 
system 
1. Introduction 
‘Linguistic diversity is part of Europe’s DNA’ is the first sentence of the introduction 
to the Eurydice thematic report published in 2023 by the European Commission, the 
executive arm of the European Union (Evropská komise, Evropská výkonná agentura 
pro vzdělávání a kulturu, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2797/146012, p. 7). Promoting 
multilingualism is one of the EU’s main objectives 
(https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/improving-quality/multilingualism/about 
multilingualism-policy). Similarly, the Council of Europe has a long-standing 
commitment to advocating for multilingualism and has issued recommendations to 
Member States in this regard (https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european 
framework-reference-languages/recommendations). This study aims to explore the 
impact of educational policies on multilingualism promotion in the Czech Republic. 
Specifically, we are interested in describing the approach to the above-mentioned 
“linguistic diversity” in the context of the Czech Republic in the last decade with a 
focus on the teaching of second foreign languages (abbreviated as FL2), i.e., German, 
French, Russian, Spanish, and Italian. As we will demonstrate in subsequent chapters, 
this decade witnessed the promotion and subsequent reconsideration of the place of 
FL2 in the curriculum. This reconsideration is notably represented by the Ministry of 
Education’s 2022 proposal to move the FL2 from the group of compulsory subjects to 
optional subjects only (i.e., compulsorily proposed by schools but optional for 
students), within a broader reform of the elementary education program 
(https://revize.rvp.cz/revize-rvp). 

In the next chapter of the study (Chapter 2), we first outline the basic picture of foreign language teaching in the Czech Republic, as seen in the above-mentioned European Commission report. In Chapter 3, we introduce the proposed reform and we describe the current place of foreign languages in the main Czech curriculum document, i.e., the Framework Educational Programme (FEP, Rámcový vzdělávací program) for elementary education, i.e., for the ISCED 1 and 2 education areas (grades covering attendance between 6–15 years of age), and partly also at ISCED 3

This study was created within the Cooperation research programme, provided by Charles University (in the fields of Linguistics and Didactics of Foreign Languages), conducted at the Faculty of Arts and at the Faculty of Pedagogy.

(15–19 years). However, we focus mainly on the compulsory education level (called “basic school”, základní škola, hereinafter elementary school), as the proposed reform of the FL2 status falls within this period. We also focus on foreign language teachers, the neuralgic point of any successful implementation of the goals of the curriculum in practice. In Chapter 4, we show what impact the current reform of the status of foreign languages could have in this situation. In the Conclusion, we suggest some solutions aiming at the development of foreign language teaching.

2

2. Main findings of the Eurydice research report In the Czech Republic, as in most European countries, English is the dominant first foreign language taught at school. According to the Eurydice report, the Czech Republic is among the 20 European countries where more than 90% of students at ISCED 1 and 2 learn English (Eurydice, 2023: 84, 86, see also Lemonnier 2022a). Moreover, the position of English is increasingly strengthened, especially at the ISCED 1 level (Eurydice, 2023: 90). Thus, other foreign languages play a crucial role in linguistic diversity, i. e., languages that complement the curriculum during the course of study, most often several years later that starts the learning of English.

In the Czech Republic (along with Denmark, Croatia, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia), German is the most common second foreign language taught at school. Other statistically observed FL2s in the Czech Republic include Russian, Spanish, French, and Italian, which, except for Russian, corresponds to the European trend (Eurydice, 2023: 89, also Andrášová 2023: 39 or Lemonnier 2022a: 15)

In the 2013/2014 school year, the Czech Republic joined the countries that have FL2 as a compulsory part of their curriculum. Students have to start learning a second foreign language from the age of 13 (i.e., the 8

th

grade of elementary school) at the latest. Some countries that have FL2 as a compulsory language start earlier (e.g., Denmark as early as age 11), some later (Hungary and Austria at age 14, Bulgaria at age 15) (Eurydice, 2023: 41). Despite this increased prominence of FL2, it does not hold an equivalent status as the first foreign language. At ISCED 1–2 levels, 15% of the teaching time is devoted to all foreign languages together in the Czech Republic (Eurydice, 2023: 129), but the time allocation is more important in FL1 than in FL2 (approximately one-third of the total language education is dedicated to FL2). Specifically, the Eurydice report cites 68 hours, i.e., 90 teaching units of 45 minutes per year (counting all 9 years of compulsory education together) of compulsory education on average, as the minimum for FL1, and only 20 hours, i.e., 27 teaching units of 45 minutes per year, for FL2. However, this disproportion is similar in all the countries surveyed in the Eurydice report and is not surprising if we consider that the FL2 instruction starts in the upper grades and often with a lower weekly lesson allocation (Eurydice, 2023: 124).

2

It should be recalled that the planned reform of the FEP concerns compulsory education, i.e. elementry schools and lower levels of víceletá gymnázia (i.e., eight and six-year grammar schools). In this study, however, we will focus on elementary schools (základní škola), because students in víceletá gymnázia represent a minority of the student population in compulsory education (approximately 4 % in 2022). Moreover, they are unlikely to be substantially affected by the potential negative effects of making FL2 an optional subject, thanks to the extra support provided by the family and the selective nature of víceletá gymnázia.

The expected level of skills in FL2 in the Czech Republic is again comparable to other European countries. At the end of the ISCED 2 level, it is A1 (in the surveyed countries referring to the Common European Framework of Reference levels, it is A1 or A2). At the end of the ISCED 3 level, it is B1 (the surveyed countries here oscillate between A2 and B1, with the exception of Italy, which requires B2) (Eurydice 2023: 133).

The context of foreign language teaching in the Czech Republic is thus clearly comparable to other European countries. We, therefore, assume that the remark towards FL2 teaching in the introduction to the English edition of the Eurydice report stating that “regarding the second foreign language more efforts are required as we do not see a noticeable improvement” can be applied to it as well (Eurydice, 2023: 6). Otherwise, the recommendation of the Council of Europe (2019) that “European countries should promote the acquisition of an additional [third] language at a level that enables them [young people] to communicate with a degree of fluency” is hard to respect (Eurydice, 2023 (English version): 7)

Regarding curriculum structure, FL2 is currently part of the Language and Communication Through Language educational area defined by the Framework Education Program for Basic Education (FEP BE). The same area also includes Czech language and literature (i.e., the so-called mother language of most students) and (first) foreign language. The subject content of FL2 is described as individual communicative competencies for the different learning levels (e.g., listening comprehension: “the student understands and responds to simple instructions and questions from the teacher, which are spoken slowly and with careful pronunciation”). Like other subjects, FL2 must develop not only its subject content but also the key competencies: learning, problem-solving, communicative, social and personal, civic, work competencies and, more recently, digital competence. In addition, there are different cross-curricular areas, including topics such as multicultural or media education (https://www.edu.cz/rvp-ramcove-vzdelavaci programy/ramcovy-vzdelavacici-program-pro-zakladni-vzdelavani-rvp-zv/). Since 2013, the Standards for Basic Education (Standardy pro ZV) have been introduced, as an appendix to the FEP BE. For each communicative competence, these Standards provide a specific example of an evaluation activity (https://digifolio.rvp.cz/view/view.php?id=9832).

3. The planned reform, the process of its preparation, and the expert public 
reactions 
The upcoming reform, referred to as a “revision” by the Czech Ministry of Education, 
Youth and Sport (MŠMT), which includes the proposal to change the status of the 
FL2, is a consequence of the application of conceptual documents issued by the 
Ministry at the end of the last decade. In particular, it is due to the Strategy for the 
Czech Republic’s Education Policy 2030+, which emphasizes the necessity of 
adapting the curriculum to a changing world. Thus, one of the most significant 
changes in this reform is the increased focus on enhancing the digital competencies of 
students in elementary education. This shift is reflected in an extended time allocation 
for subjects related to information technology and the introduction of a new digital 
competence among the key competencies. 

As for foreign languages, only on page 92 the document mentions that “the content of the Framework Educational Program for Basic Education will be innovated in key competences, with a priority focus on the following key areas: mother language and foreign language, mathematics and science (STEM) and the use of digital

technologies” (https://www.msmt.cz/uploads/Brozura_S2030_online_CZ.pdf). Subsequently, in the specific guidelines for the revision of the FEP based on Strategy 2030+, it is mentioned that the FL2 will have a different curricular position. It will no longer be a compulsory subject but will become a mandatory elective subject, which means that schools will have to offer it as one of the elective options alongside non linguistic subjects. This change implies that students will not be required to choose the FL2, and schools must provide an alternative to the FL2. The specific nature of this alternative has not been specified yet, but it is expected to be a technically oriented subject, a sports-related subject, or additional English classes.

By this new approach, the designers of the reform intend to support motivated students willing to learn the FL2, and, on the other hand, to allow others to choose another subject instead of the FL2 and to focus on the first foreign language only. It is also intended to be an easier route for students with specific educational needs. Nev
